period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 4 periods = 160 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

periods.activity_title: Meet the Animals: First Encounter with the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — What do You do? (pp.34–35): call-and-response recitation with actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud from Textbook pp.34–35, pointing to each animal stanza. Students listen and observe the repeating question and each animal's answer.

Teacher models the call-and-response: teacher asks 'Who are you? And what do you do?' for the birds stanza and students echo the animal reply. The class works through all six animals — birds, monkeys, dogs, cats, elephants, lions — in this pattern.

Fun with Words — What do You do? ("call-and-response chant, six animals, whole class"). Students are divided into two groups: one group chants the question lines and the other chants each animal's reply, switching roles midway.
Quick round: teacher points to individual students or rows and asks 'Who are you? And what do you do?' — each student or group replies as a chosen animal from memory, without the book.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's anaphoric refrain — 'Who are you? And what do you do?' — makes it easy for students to join in almost immediately; encourage full-voice participation from the first round. If some students are uncertain of an animal's response lines, accept partial replies and build confidence before expecting the full stanza.

periods.activity_title: Act It Out: Animal Actions and Call-and-Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — What do You do? (pp.34–35): role-play with animal actions added to each stanza.

time_bands.activity: Brief re-recite of the full poem chorally from Textbook pp.34–35 to warm voices and revive the rhythm. Teacher taps the beat lightly while students chant.

Teacher assigns each row or group one animal — birds, monkeys, dogs, cats, elephants, or lions. Each group decides on a body action that matches their animal's lines: for example, flapping arms for birds chirping and singing, or swinging arms for monkeys jumping and swinging.

Fun with Words — What do You do? ("role-play: animal groups add actions to their stanza"). Class performs the full poem in call-and-response: the questioning side chants while the animal group performs their action and speaks their reply. Rotate so every group performs at least once.

Whole-class debrief: teacher asks each group to say aloud, in one sentence, what their animal does — for example, 'Cats mew in the dark.' Students check their sentence matches the poem's words exactly.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together in the previous encounter, students can now focus on connecting each action verb to a physical movement — chirp-and-sing, jump-and-swing, run-and-bark, mew, raise trunks, roar-and-hunt. Watch that students are using the correct verb for their animal; the debrief sentence is a good quick check.
materials: Open floor space or aisle for movement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — What do You do? (pp.34–35): paired call-and-response using all six animal stanzas.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models paired call-and-response with a student volunteer: teacher asks the question lines and the student replies as one animal, then roles swap. Students observe the pattern before trying themselves.

Fun with Words — What do You do? ("paired call-and-response, all six animals"). Students work in pairs: partner A asks both question lines for each stanza, partner B replies as the animal. They go through all six animals in order, then swap roles. Books may be open for support.

Selected pairs perform for the class without books. Teacher listens for correct animal names and matching action words — chirp and sing, jump and swing, run and bark, mew in the dark, raise trunks, roar and hunt — and gives a brief nod or gentle correction after each pair finishes.

Whole-class close: teacher says an action word from the poem (for example, 'roar') and asks students to call out the animal — quick oral round to consolidate the action-verb-to-animal link before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: Having performed the poem in groups with actions, students are now ready to handle the full sequence in pairs without group support. Encourage pairs to use natural speaking voices rather than singing or shouting; the goal is fluent, confident recall of each animal's two-line answer.

periods.activity_title: Bringing the Poem to Life: Chapter Synthesis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — What do You do? (pp.34–35): whole-class performed recitation presenting all six animals with actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a quick whole-class question: for each of the six animals in the poem — birds, monkeys, dogs, cats, elephants, lions — students call out what that animal does. This revisits the action verbs (chirp and sing, jump and swing, run and bark, mew in the dark, raise trunks, roar and hunt) that the poem centres on.

Each group (one per animal) prepares a short oral presentation of their stanza: they choose a speaker to say the reply lines, agree on a group action to perform, and practise once quietly. All work happens inside these minutes — no prior preparation is assumed.

Groups present in poem order — birds first, then monkeys, dogs, cats, elephants, lions. The rest of the class chants the question lines ('Who are you? And what do you do?') before each group performs. Teacher draws attention to how the repeating question and the different animal answers create the poem's rhythm.

Teacher closes by asking: what is special about the way this poem asks its questions? Students share briefly — guiding them to notice that every animal gets the same two questions but gives its own answer. Teacher names this repeating pattern (the refrain) in simple terms.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the poem's central ideas — the anaphoric refrain, the six animals, and their defining action verbs — through a performed oral presentation. The closing discussion about the repeating question pattern gives students a simple concept (refrain) to carry forward from their work on this poem.
materials: Open floor space for group performance

items.item_stem: Listen carefully. Your teacher will say the name of an animal from the poem 'What do You do?'. Choose what that animal does.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be recalling birds rather than cats, confusing two early stanzas.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be recalling lions, the final stanza, rather than cats.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may be recalling monkeys, mixing up the animals' action lines.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will ask you: 'Who are you? And what do you do?' Choose any one animal from the poem and speak its answer aloud. Add a body action that matches what the animal does.

expected_elements: Names the correct animal from the poem.
Speaks the matching action words clearly.
